title: Tobacco use and readiness to change

patient.name: Marcus Hale
patient.presenting_concern: Discussion of tobacco use during a routine visit

learning_goal: Assess readiness, explore sustain talk and support autonomy; the patient remains unwilling to quit. Do not score success by agreement to cessation.
educator_description: Marcus Hale is a 42-year-old man who smokes one pack a day. He is not willing to quit smoking. He works rotating shifts, uses cigarettes for stress relief, and had a difficult previous quit attempt. The goal is to explore his willingness to change without pressuring him.
teaching_notes: Use the fixed suggested sequence for a coherent rehearsal.
This is an authored demonstration, not a diagnosis or grading engine.

dialogue.student: Hello, I am the medical student working with your clinician. Would it be okay to talk about smoking for a few minutes?
dialogue.patient: We can talk, but I am telling you now: I am not quitting.

dialogue.student: What does smoking do for you during a usual day?
dialogue.patient: I smoke about a pack a day. With rotating shifts, those breaks are how I settle down.

dialogue.student: How do you feel about making a change right now?
dialogue.patient: I do not want to change. I know people say it is bad, but quitting is not on my list right now.

chart.label: Patient-stated readiness
chart.text: The patient explicitly declines cessation at this visit. Readiness is not inferred from agreement to receive information.

dialogue.student: You really need to stop; could you set a quit date this week?
dialogue.patient: No. That is what everyone says. If this is going to be another lecture, I would rather leave.

dialogue.student: I pushed ahead of where you are. You get to decide. What was difficult the last time you tried?
dialogue.patient: I barely slept, I was irritable at work, and I went back to smoking. I do not want to go through that again.

dialogue.student: It sounds like smoking helps you manage stress, and the last attempt was miserable. What matters most to you at the moment?
dialogue.patient: Keeping my job and getting through my shifts. My daughter hates the smell, but that does not mean I am ready to quit.

dialogue.student: Would you like information about support available if you ever choose to revisit this?
dialogue.patient: You can give me something to look at, but I am not promising to call anyone or take medicine.

dialogue.student: I hear that you are not ready. We can revisit it when you want. Is there anything you want us to understand before we finish?
dialogue.patient: Just do not make every visit about cigarettes. I want help with my health without being judged.

debrief.question: Compare the patient response before and after the quit-date question. What changed in the conversation?
Which of the patient priorities could you reflect back without treating them as a commitment to change?
How would you distinguish permission to receive information from willingness to start treatment?
What would a useful closing plan look like if the patient still declines change?
